*: Light from one visual field falls on the nasal retina of the eye on that side and the temporal retina of the other eye, where photoreceptors drive the bipolar cells (1st-order neurons).
Retinal ganglion cell axons (2nd order) leave each eye in its optic nerve and run back to the optic chiasm.
In the optic chiasm the fibres from the nasal half of each retina cross to the opposite optic tract.
The fibres from the temporal half of each retina pass the chiasm without crossing.
Each optic tract now carries the opposite visual field from both eyes, back to the lateral geniculate nucleus.
The 3rd-order cell body sits in the lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus, where the retinotopic map is kept.
Optic radiation fibres for the lower visual field run back‹ through the parietal lobe› to the superior bank of the calcarine sulcus (cuneus).
Fibres for the upper visual field loop forward into the temporal lobe‹ (Meyer's loop)› before running back to the inferior bank (lingual gyrus).
V1 lines the calcarine sulcus: the upper field lands below it and the lower field above it, in the hemisphere opposite the field.
Light falls on the retina of ONE eye.
Retinal ganglion cell axons carry the signal back in the optic nerve.
Instead of the LGN, these fibres reach the pretectal nucleus of the midbrain, near the superior colliculus.
Nasal fibres cross in the chiasm, so both pretectal nuclei are driven, and each projects to the Edinger-Westphal nuclei of both sides.
The parasympathetic preganglionic cell bodies of CN III sit in both Edinger-Westphal nuclei.
Preganglionic axons run in the oculomotor nerve to the ciliary ganglion; short postganglionic fibres reach the sphincter pupillae.
Both pupils constrict (consensual reflex); the same pathway constricts the pupil in accommodation.
Voluntary gaze starts in the frontal eye field (BA 8) of the hemisphere opposite the direction of gaze.
FEF axons cross to the opposite PPRF near the abducens nucleus; the abducens nucleus also sends axons across into the MLF up to the other oculomotor nucleus.
Lower motor neurons sit in the abducens nucleus (gaze side) and the oculomotor nucleus (other side).
The abducens nerve drives the lateral rectus of the gaze-side eye; the oculomotor nerve drives the medial rectus of the other eye.
Lateral and medial rectus contract together: conjugate gaze toward the side opposite the active FEF.
Sound moves the hair cells of the cochlea.
The hair cells drive the peripheral process of a bipolar neuron in the cochlea.
The 1st-order cell body sits in the spiral ganglion inside the cochlea.
Its axon runs in the cochlear part of CN VIII to the cochlear nuclei of the rostral medulla.
The 2nd-order cell bodies sit in the cochlear nuclei.
Their axons climb the lateral brainstem on both sides, some crossing in the pons, to the inferior colliculus.
The inferior colliculus of the midbrain is the next relay.
From the inferior colliculus the signal goes to the medial geniculate nucleus of the thalamus.
The medial geniculate nucleus is the auditory relay of the thalamus.
Its axons pass through the internal capsule to the transverse temporal gyrus.
The primary auditory cortex (BA 41, 42) lies in the transverse temporal gyrus; each side hears both ears.
Head movement and gravity move the hair cells of the semicircular canals (rotation) and the utricle and saccule (linear acceleration).
The 1st-order axon leaves the labyrinth in the vestibular nerve.
The 1st-order cell body sits in the vestibular ganglion of CN VIII.
The axon enters the brainstem and synapses in the vestibular nuclei.
Some axons go straight to the flocculonodular lobe of the cerebellum by the inferior cerebellar peduncle.
The 2nd-order cell bodies sit in the vestibular nuclei of the pons and medulla.
Ascending fibres in the MLF reach the abducens and oculomotor nuclei: the vestibulo-ocular reflex turns the eyes opposite to the head.
The vestibulospinal tract descends to the ventral horn for trunk muscles, posture and righting.
Other fibres ascend to the thalamus and on to the cortex for conscious perception of movement.
